points: Direct-contact module fitted with a polytetrafluoroethylene membrane; feed temperature 60 degrees Celsius and permeate temperature 20 degrees Celsius
Initial permeate flux 18.5 kilograms per square metre per hour
Feed sodium chloride concentration 35 grams per litre; salt rejection 99.8 percent
Continuous run of 72 hours; final flux 14.2 kilograms per square metre per hour, a decline of 23.2 percent from the initial value
Each condition run in 4 replicates; flux standard deviation 0.9 kilograms per square metre per hour at the initial condition
definitions: permeate flux = mass of water crossing a unit area of membrane in a unit time
salt rejection = percentage of feed salt retained on the feed side of the membrane
membrane distillation = separation process in which a hydrophobic microporous membrane passes water vapour and retains liquid water
limits: Flux values apply to sodium chloride feeds without surfactants at the stated temperature pair
figures: Fig. 1: permeate flux and salt rejection over the continuous run, with error bars from the replicate standard deviation
prose: Permeate flux (permeate flux: the mass of water crossing a unit area of membrane in a unit time) reached 18.5 kilograms per square metre per hour at a feed temperature of 60 degrees Celsius and a permeate temperature of 20 degrees Celsius. The module ran in direct-contact configuration, with hot feed on one side of a polytetrafluoroethylene membrane and cold permeate on the other side. Membrane distillation (membrane distillation: a separation process in which a hydrophobic microporous membrane passes water vapour and retains liquid water) carried water across the membrane as vapour, and the vapour condensed in the permeate stream. Feed solution contained sodium chloride at 35 grams per litre, and salt rejection (salt rejection: the percentage of feed salt retained on the feed side of the membrane) held at 99.8 percent across the full run. Permeate mass accumulated in a tank on a balance, and permeate conductivity gave the salt passage after calibration against standard solutions. Flux declined over 72 hours of continuous operation and reached 14.2 kilograms per square metre per hour at the end of the run, a decline of 23.2 percent from the initial value. The decline followed deposit growth on the membrane surface, and deposit growth raised the resistance to vapour transport through the membrane pores. Feed circulation held the channel velocity steady through the run, and temperature sensors at the module inlets and outlets recorded the thermal state of both streams. Each condition ran in 4 replicates, and the standard deviation of the flux across replicates was 0.9 kilograms per square metre per hour at the initial condition. Replicate spread stayed narrow beside the decline across the run, and the decline appears in every replicate record with the same direction and a similar rate. Flux values at the stated temperatures apply to sodium chloride feeds without surfactants, and surfactant-bearing feeds fall outside the tested range. Cleaning trials stand outside the present results, and the deposit composition awaits analysis by surface methods. Fig. 1 shows permeate flux and salt rejection over the continuous run, with error bars drawn from the replicate standard deviation.

points: Biochar from pyrolysis at 550 degrees Celsius, applied at 20 tonnes per hectare
Field trial with 12 plots on a single soil type, biochar plots and control plots in randomised blocks
Soil organic carbon in biochar plots rose from 1.8 percent to 2.3 percent over 3 years, a gain of 0.5 percentage points
Retention of applied biochar carbon in the soil reached 68 percent at the final sampling
Soil pH in biochar plots moved from 5.6 to 6.1
definitions: biochar = carbon-rich solid produced by heating biomass with limited oxygen
soil organic carbon = carbon held in soil organic matter, reported as a mass percentage of dry soil
mineral-associated organic matter = fraction of soil organic matter bound to mineral surfaces
limits: Results apply to the single soil type and the climate of the trial site
prose: Biochar (biochar: the carbon-rich solid produced by heating biomass with limited oxygen) came from pyrolysis at 550 degrees Celsius and entered the field trial at 20 tonnes per hectare. The trial held 12 plots on a single soil type, with biochar plots and control plots arranged in randomised blocks across the field. Surface soil came from sampling points distributed across each plot, and composite samples carried the plot values into the analysis. Soil organic carbon (soil organic carbon: the carbon held in soil organic matter, reported as a mass percentage of dry soil) rose from 1.8 percent to 2.3 percent in the biochar plots over 3 years, a gain of 0.5 percentage points. Control plots held near the starting value across the same period, and the contrast between the treatments widened at each sampling round. Carbon analysis ran by dry combustion on air-dried and ground subsamples, with carbonate removal before analysis on the limed plots. Retention of the applied biochar carbon in the soil reached 68 percent at the final sampling, and the retained fraction sat mainly in mineral-associated organic matter (mineral-associated organic matter: the fraction of soil organic matter bound to mineral surfaces). The mineral-associated pool turns over slowly, and residence in that pool matches the persistence the carbon balance records. Soil acidity, reported as pH (pH: the negative logarithm of the hydrogen ion activity in the soil suspension), moved from 5.6 to 6.1 in the biochar plots across the trial. The pH shift followed the alkalinity of the ash fraction in the biochar, and control plots showed no matching shift. Crop management, fertiliser practice and tillage stayed uniform across plots, and yield records showed no penalty on the biochar plots. Results apply to the single soil type and the climate of the trial site, and transfer to soils with a different clay content or rainfall regime awaits trials on those soils. Longer runs at the same site will test whether the retention figure holds as the labile fraction of the biochar declines.

points: Worked example pipe: radius 0.05 metres, length 2 metres, pressure drop 1200 pascals, oil viscosity 0.1 pascal seconds
Wall shear stress from the overall balance: 15 pascals
Maximum velocity at the centreline from the integrated profile: 3.75 metres per second
Mean velocity, half the maximum for the parabolic profile: 1.875 metres per second
definitions: shear stress = tangential force per unit area exerted by one fluid layer on the next, in pascals
radial coordinate = distance from the pipe centreline, in metres
dynamic viscosity = ratio of shear stress to velocity gradient in the fluid, in pascal seconds
momentum shell = thin cylindrical layer of fluid at a stated radius, used as the control volume for the balance
limits: The balance applies to steady, laminar, incompressible flow in a horizontal circular pipe, with no slip at the wall
prose: This tutorial builds the velocity profile for laminar pipe flow from a momentum balance on a cylindrical shell, and the worked example at the end gives a profile you can check against the overall force balance on the same pipe. Start with the geometry. The pipe is circular, the flow is steady, and the velocity points along the pipe axis with a magnitude that changes only with radial position. A momentum shell (momentum shell: a thin cylindrical layer of fluid at a stated radius, used as the control volume for the balance) sits at a chosen radius, and the shell has the pipe length and a small thickness. Pressure acts on the two end faces of the shell, and shear stress (shear stress: the tangential force per unit area exerted by one fluid layer on the next, in pascals) acts on the inner and outer cylindrical faces. Steady flow holds no accumulation of momentum in the shell, and the pressure forces and the shear forces on the shell balance. Writing that balance and shrinking the shell thickness gives a relation between the radial coordinate (radial coordinate: the distance from the pipe centreline, in metres) and the shear stress: shear stress grows in direct proportion to radius, from zero at the centreline to a maximum at the wall. The constitutive relation for a Newtonian fluid ties shear stress to the velocity gradient through dynamic viscosity (dynamic viscosity: the ratio of shear stress to velocity gradient in the fluid, in pascal seconds), and substitution turns the stress relation into a differential equation for velocity. Integration with the no-slip condition at the wall and a finite velocity at the centreline gives the parabolic profile. Work through the example with oil in a pipe of radius 0.05 metres and length 2 metres, a pressure drop of 1200 pascals, and a viscosity of 0.1 pascal seconds. The overall balance on the whole pipe gives the wall shear stress directly, and the value is 15 pascals. The integrated profile gives a maximum velocity at the centreline of 3.75 metres per second, and the mean velocity is 1.875 metres per second. Check the result in two places: the wall stress from the profile gradient matches the overall balance, and the mean velocity sits at half the maximum, as a parabolic profile requires. The balance applies to steady, laminar, incompressible flow in a horizontal circular pipe, with no slip at the wall, and turbulent flow needs a different stress model.

points: Supported ruthenium catalyst bed; ammonia conversion 98 percent at 650 degrees Celsius
Hydrogen output 12 kilograms per hour at the reactor outlet
Hydrogen purity 99.9 percent after purification by pressure swing adsorption
Catalyst activity held across a stability run of 500 hours
definitions: ammonia cracking = decomposition of ammonia into hydrogen and nitrogen over a catalyst
conversion = percentage of the ammonia feed decomposed in a single pass through the reactor
prose: Hydrogen supply from a liquid carrier needs a release step with high conversion and a clean product stream. Ammonia cracking (ammonia cracking: the decomposition of ammonia into hydrogen and nitrogen over a catalyst) over a supported ruthenium catalyst bed reached a conversion (conversion: the percentage of the ammonia feed decomposed in a single pass through the reactor) of 98 percent at 650 degrees Celsius. Hydrogen output at the reactor outlet reached 12 kilograms per hour, and purification by pressure swing adsorption (pressure swing adsorption: a cyclic separation in which a bed adsorbs the unwanted components under pressure and releases the components on depressurisation) held hydrogen purity at 99.9 percent. Catalyst activity held across a stability run of 500 hours, with conversion at the end of the run matching the opening value within the repeatability of the gas analysis. Reactor heat came from electric elements around the bed, and temperature control held the bed at the stated value through load changes in the feed. The reactor and the purification train ran as a single unit during the stability run, and product composition came from continuous gas analysis at the outlet. The results place ammonia cracking at a scale suited to distributed hydrogen supply, with conversion and purity held together over a long run.
